title: Job training but no meal plans or sports: A new college model
text:
Job training but no meal plans or sports: A new college model
A new Vermont engineering college offers a more economical path to a degree and a job.
Up the road from the Vermont State House, in the small city of Montpelier, a group of business leaders and educators are planning to launch what they hope will be a solution to what they see as a need in American higher education.
Greenway Institute, a new nonprofit engineering college that will combine two years of classroom education with two years of paid work experience for students, will open its doors in fall 2027 to a class of about 50 students. It is an effort, says co-founder Mark Somerville, to lower the cost of college while fixing what he and others say is a broken financial model that offers a poor value proposition for students.
“What if we stopped treating work as sort of an adjunct to education and instead made it an integral part of education?” says Mr. Somerville, president of Greenway.
Colleges face plunging enrollment while students balk at sky-high tuition. Some higher education innovators are offering models that strip college down to the essentials.
Over the last decade, about 150 colleges have shut down, merged, or announced plans to close, including at least seven in the Green Mountain State. Rising costs and competition for students are straining college budgets, while declining birth rates threaten to further shrink the pool of prospective students. Greenway is among 15 startup institutions participating in Duke University’s Future Universities Alliance, a network of 49 schools across 23 countries exploring new approaches to higher education.
“Starting from scratch has the advantage that you can try to build exactly what you want to build without any history or legacy structures being in the way,” says Robert Kelchen, a professor of higher education at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. “But on the other hand, you’re starting without anyone knowing who you are [and] without accreditation.”
Greenway’s model draws on approaches already used by other engineering institutions. Iron Range Engineering in Minnesota, for example, integrates work-based learning into their program. The school allows students to work industry jobs ranging from, but not limited to, clean energy to aerospace engineering during their junior and senior years, while earning academic credit. Olin College of Engineering in Massachusetts, which Mr. Somerville helped develop, centers its curriculum on project-based and collaborative learning. Students work directly with users and communities to solve real-world problems.
Mr. Somerville notes that 77% of recent graduates surveyed in 2025 say they learned more in six months at their job than in their entire four-year education.
Jody Jessup-Anger, department chair and professor of higher education at Marquette University in Wisconsin, says that having a model with a clear career pathway would be good for students “at a time when a lot of students are feeling pretty insecure about life after their collegiate experience.”
Greenway’s founders bring experience in business, government, and higher education. They include a clean-energy entrepreneur, a former Vermont secretary of education, and a former engineering college provost. Together, they hope to make engineering degrees more affordable and better prepare students for the workforce.
For Greenway, reinventing the college experience also means rethinking its cost. The institution plans to charge less than $25,000 in annual tuition, about $15,000 below the national average for private nonprofit four-year colleges. Its founders say students can make back that expense through their work-integrated years. The average hourly wage for those jobs that are part of their academic program, called co-ops, is around $24.46, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers. At that rate, students working full time throughout the year could earn roughly $50,000 annually.
Troy McBride, one of Greenway’s co-founders, says a key part of that approach is limiting students’ time on campus and offering fewer amenities. The institution plans to strip programs such as varsity sports and meal plans, which helps reduce expenses associated with maintaining a residential college.
But Mr. Kelchen says the bigger challenge may be the cost of teaching engineering itself, adding that convincing students to enroll in an institution without an established track record can be difficult.
Engineering programs, Mr. Kelchen says, typically need expensive facilities, such as robotics or electrical engineering labs. And Greenway’s emphasis on hands-on, project-based learning could make instruction more costly because it requires more individual attention from professors. Greenway says that by having its students do their more advanced engineering work at companies, the school avoids the need for expensive facilities.
New schools, Mr. Kelchen says, face the question: “Do we even know if this college is going to be around for their whole time that they’re enrolled?”
Greenway has already tested parts of its proposed models through two pilot semesters in partnership with Elizabethtown College in Pennsylvania. In 2023, a small group of engineering students from Elizabethtown spent a semester at Greenway’s Vermont campus. Rather than sitting in traditional classrooms and listening to lectures, students spent their time working on projects while earning college credits. A second cohort in 2025 tested the employment-based model, working nearly full time with mentorship from Greenway’s faculty. Since the work-based years are remote, students aren’t limited to work with only local engineering firms in Vermont.
Jazz Gonzalez, a recent graduate from Elizabethtown who participated in one of the pilots, says the transition from traditional classroom instruction to Greenway’s project-based learning was initially difficult.
“Normally during college, they kind of tell you what you need to know versus Greenway where they say, ‘OK, you choose what topic you want to learn and we’ll help you in trying to learn it,’” says Mr. Gonzalez, who now works as a technical support specialist at Phoenix Contact USA, a company whose products help with industrial automation, and is part of Greenway’s presidential advisory board.
But after a month, the approach became more natural, allowing students to explore engineering concepts through hands-on projects, including building a prototype solar-powered traffic light.
“It sticks with you so much longer,” he says.
